metaDescription: Six compact handheld leaf blowers compared by weight, battery, tube design and airflow, from corded 7-amp models to 2.7 lb cordless turbo jets.
expertTake: The Makita DUB185Z is the best compact blower because its variable trigger and three volume settings give real control, if you already own 18V LXT batteries. The SEYVUM 20V kit is the value pick with two batteries and a two-piece tube. Skip a small blower if your leaf load is heavy or wet, because a compact motor pushes only so much air.
introParagraphs: A small leaf blower is defined by its body: a handheld motor you can pick up with one hand, hang on a hook and carry to a patio without planning. It trades airflow for convenience, and it is the right tool for decks, porches, garages and tidy lawns.

The things that matter are weight, how the tube comes apart, how long the battery lasts on a normal setting and whether the speed control has any finesse. Peak numbers on a compact tool are the least reliable figures on the box.

products.name: Makita DUB185Z 18V LXT cordless blower, 3 volume settings, tool only
products.description:
What sets the DUB185Z apart is control, which is rarely found at this size. A variable-speed trigger sits on top of three air volume settings, so you choose low, medium or high and then feather the trigger within it. That two-layer control is the difference between nudging dust from a workbench and clearing a patio.

It also doubles as a vacuum with a dust bag, a feature most compact blowers lack. That makes it handy in a garage or workshop, not just a yard. The cost is the entry: it is sold tool only, so you need LXT batteries and a charger, which is cheap if you already own a Makita drill and expensive if you do not.

The tool is simple and well-built. Clear the intake, wipe the housing, and store it on the shelf with the battery off. Check the dust bag for tears before each vacuum job, and keep the nozzle free of grit. If you use it in a workshop, empty the dust bag outdoors, since fine sawdust is easy to inhale and settles back on benches. Keep one spare battery charged so the tool is ready when a quick cleanup is needed, which is how a compact blower earns its keep.
products.bestFor: Makita battery owners who want control in a compact tool.
pros: Variable trigger on top of three settings
Also works as a vacuum with a dust bag

products.name: SEYVUM 20V cordless blower, 350 CFM, 150 MPH, two 2.0Ah, 2-piece tube

specList.label: Tube
specList.value: Two sections, usable together or separately

products.description:
SEYVUM gives you a complete compact kit: 350 CFM and 150 MPH from a 15,000 rpm motor, two 2.0Ah batteries and a fast charger. The tube comes in two sections that attach for a long reach or work separately for a short nozzle, a small design detail that matters when you need to reach under a bench or into a corner.

Its numbers are honest for the size: 150 MPH is a gentle speed that will not strip mulch, and 350 CFM is enough for dry leaves on a patio. Against the BLACK+DECKER corded unit it moves roughly double the air, and against the JAGROM it has about twice the volume.

The batteries are small, so the claim of long runtime is on the lowest setting. Charge them after use, store them indoors and avoid leaving them on the charger. Wipe the nozzle and check the tube joint for grit. Because the packs are small, learn how many minutes you actually get on your usual setting and plan jobs to fit, rather than discovering the limit halfway across a patio. A short charge between jobs is one of the pleasant things about a compact tool.
products.bestFor: A compact household kit that stores in a cupboard.
pros: 350 CFM and 150 MPH from a compact body
Two-piece tube for long or short reach
Two batteries and a fast charger

products.name: SEESE Turbo Jet cordless blower, 600 CFM, 2.7 lb brushless
products.description:
SEESE is the lightest tool here at 2.7 pounds, and the maker contrasts that with 6 to 10 pound conventional blowers that tire your arm. A pure-copper brushless motor is described, and it quotes 600 CFM, the highest claimed volume among the compact tools in this guide.

It is a turbo jet in format, which means a narrow, fast stream rather than a wide column. That is excellent for workshops, decks and stuck debris and less good for sweeping a lawn. It also handles wood shavings and dust, so it earns its place in a garage.

Treat the intake as a filter: wipe dust from the grille, store it in a bag and do not run it near wet leaves. A light tool has less margin for abuse, so keep it away from water. A bag with a drawstring keeps lint and sawdust off the intake between uses, and a hook on the wall keeps it off the floor where it can suck up debris on the next start. Avoid blowing straight at anyone, because a narrow jet at this speed can carry grit into eyes.
products.bestFor: Workshops, decks and anyone for whom weight is the priority.
cons: Narrow jet is poor for lawns

products.name: laapee 20V cordless blower, two 4.0Ah batteries, turbo motor
products.description:
laapee pairs a compact body with larger-than-usual batteries: two 4.0Ah packs and a fast charger. That means a small blower that can run longer than the SEYVUM's 2.0Ah pair, which matters for a driveway or a long path. A simple switch increases or decreases airflow.

The listing does not give a CFM figure in the data here, so judge it by the motor type and the battery capacity. It is a straightforward, light tool, a good fit for owners who find small packs frustrating.

As with any compact cordless blower, store the packs indoors, wipe the intake clear and charge after use. If you buy it for a larger job, keep one pack on the charger while using the other, which turns two 4.0Ah packs into near-continuous running. A quick test on a corner of the patio will tell you whether the airflow suits your leaves before the first big session.
products.bestFor: Owners who want a small blower with a longer runtime.

products.name: JAGROM 20V cordless blower, 180 CFM, 130 MPH, two 2.0Ah, two tubes
products.description:
JAGROM is the simplest and lowest-power cordless blower in the roundup: 180 CFM and 130 MPH, with two 2.0Ah batteries and a charger. The maker claims more than 30 minutes of runtime, and two tubes install without tools, so you can clean the floor and reach higher spots.

That modest output is both its limit and its benefit. It is a gentle blower for garages, porches and short paths, and it will not scatter mulch. It cannot move a pile of leaves in any hurry, so it suits light daily sweeping rather than seasonal clear-outs.

Store the batteries indoors and charge after use. The two tubes are a simple feature, but check the joint for grit and do not force a misaligned tube. Pull the tubes apart and wipe them occasionally, because dust works into the joint and makes the next connection stiff. Keep it away from heavy wet leaves, which are beyond its small motor.
products.bestFor: Light daily sweeping of garages, porches and paths.
cons: Only 180 CFM, slow on leaf drifts

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 7-Amp corded blower, 180 MPH, 180 CFM
products.description:
If a cordless pack is a nuisance, a 7 amp corded blower is the simple answer. It makes 180 CFM and 180 MPH, a small, brisk jet that handles dry leaves on a stoop and grit in a garage. Cord retention built into the handle keeps the extension cord from pulling out.

The tradeoff against the cordless kits is range and volume, but not durability: with no battery to degrade, a corded blower usually outlasts a cordless one. Against the SEYVUM it moves about half the air, so large jobs take longer.

Maintenance is minimal. Use a 14 or 16 gauge outdoor cord, inspect it for cuts, clear the intake and store the tool dry. It is the cheapest long-term option here. Coil the cord loosely over a hook when you finish, never tightly around the handle, and keep a short extension at the door so you are not hunting for one each time. If the cord ever feels warm in use, it is too thin for the run.
products.bestFor: Owners with an outlet nearby who want zero battery fuss.
pros: No battery to age or charge
180 MPH is brisk for dry leaves

buyingCriteria.explanation: A compact blower is held at arm's length, so weight matters more than at first glance. The SEESE at 2.7 pounds is the lightest here. The motor and battery sit at the back of the tool in most designs, so check that the balance is not nose-heavy.

A compact motor cannot move the same air as a backpack. JAGROM's 180 CFM and SEYVUM's 350 CFM are realistic for the class, while 600 CFM claims on tiny jets are a peak figure. Treat any number above 500 CFM on a 2.7 pound tool with caution.
Small tools often ship with 2.0Ah packs that run down in 15 to 25 minutes. The laapee's two 4.0Ah packs run roughly twice as long. If you plan any driveway work, buy larger packs or a second set.
Two-section tubes, as on the SEYVUM and JAGROM, let you work long or short. A fixed short nozzle can be fine, but it limits reach. Check that the tube clicks together firmly and does not wobble.

A variable trigger plus three settings on the Makita gives real control, while a simple two-speed switch does not. For beds, pots and delicate surfaces, fine control prevents scattering. Without it you will be choosing between too soft and too hard, and you will end up either chasing leaves or blasting grit around the patio.

A small blower should store in a cupboard. The Makita shares 18V LXT batteries with other tools, while the others are standalone. If you already own a platform, a tool-only blower is a cheap add, and a second tool on the same battery means one charger serves both.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated weight, balance and how the tool sits in the hand. The 2.7 lb SEESE scored best on lightness, while the Makita scored best on control.

howWeEvaluated.title: Airflow against class
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet, we compared claimed CFM with the size of the tool. Moderate claims such as SEYVUM's 350 CFM were treated as more credible than 600 CFM on a very light body.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery value
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted what ships in the box and pack capacity, from 2.0Ah to 4.0Ah, as well as the tool-only Makita.

howWeEvaluated.title: Tube and versatility
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared tube designs and extra functions such as the Makita's vacuum mode.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership cost
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared relative tiers and long-term costs, including the corded unit's lack of a battery.

cards.label: Corded
cards.text: The BLACK+DECKER never runs down and has no battery to age. The cord limits range, and it can snag on furniture. It suits small areas near an outlet.

cards.label: Cordless
cards.text: The Makita, SEYVUM, SEESE, laapee and JAGROM go anywhere. Packs run down and age. They suit patios, driveways and out front.

howToChoose.note: Choose corded for a fixed spot near an outlet; choose cordless for flexibility.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A narrow jet, a vacuum mode and speed control. Dust and shavings need a focused stream. A tool that can also vacuum earns its place.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Makita DUB185Z with its vacuum mode and the SEESE turbo jet are the best for workshops. The JAGROM suits light garage sweeping.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want control, a platform or a quality build. The Makita DUB185Z rewards owners of LXT batteries.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your jobs are light. The JAGROM or BLACK+DECKER does the work at a low tier.

maintenance.why: Dust and lint clog small intakes and heat the motor. A clean intake keeps airflow steady.
Heat and cold shorten pack life. Store at partial charge.
Two-piece tubes wear and wobble. Clean grit from the joint.
A full bag cuts suction. The Makita's bag should be inspected for tears.
A damaged cord is a shock risk. Replace it.

faq.q: What is a small leaf blower best for?
faq.a: Decks, porches, garages and light lawn work. It is not for heavy leaf loads, large lawns or soaked piles, where a bigger blower is the right tool. Choose by weight and control, and think about where the tool will live between jobs, because a blower that is easy to grab gets used and one buried in a shed does not.

faq.q: Corded or cordless for a small blower?
faq.a: Corded avoids batteries and costs less to own, but limits range. Cordless is more flexible. Pick by how far you need to go, and by whether you would rather spend a minute on a cord or a minute on a charger.

The JAGROM and BLACK+DECKER sit at lower tiers, the SEYVUM and laapee in the middle and the Makita depends on batteries. Spend for control, not peak numbers, since a small tool that you can steer finely beats a louder one you cannot.

faq.q: Will a small blower handle wet leaves?
faq.a: Not well. A compact motor lacks the volume for wet mats. Wait for dry leaves or use a larger tool, because pushing a small motor against a wet mat only heats it and drains the pack for little gain.

faq.q: How long will the battery last?
faq.a: A 2.0Ah pack gives around 15 to 25 minutes at mid speed. A 4.0Ah pack roughly doubles that. Buy a second pack for longer jobs, and label the packs so you rotate them evenly.

Quieter than gas, but a high-speed fan is still loud. Use the lowest effective setting and avoid early hours, and keep in mind that the shrill note of a high-speed turbine carries further than the low rumble of a larger blower.
